newsitem.title: UK: IRA attacks spark fresh N.Irish security demands.
newsitem.headline: IRA attacks spark fresh N.Irish security demands.

text.p: Northern Ireland's Protestant politicians called for stepped-up security measures on Wednesday after a bomb attack on police that looked like part of an escalating campaign by Irish guerrillas against British rule.
Royal Ulster Constabulary sources said officers narrowly escaped injury late on Tuesday when a device planted at a roadside in Londonderry exploded as their armoured cars passed.

"Clearly, police had a lucky escape," a security source said as RUC and British army personnel moved in during daylight to search the scene, a suburb of the city near the border with the Irish Republic, to establish what device was used.
Security sources suspect that the Irish Republican Army (IRA) carried out the attack, probably using a home-made horizontally launched mortar bomb or a landmine.

The ambush, which was condemned by the main Irish Catholic nationalist Social Democratic and Labour Party, came 36 hours after an IRA rocket attack injured a policeman in a security hut at the province's heavily protected chief law courts in Belfast.
That incident added to tension after a spate of recent attacks and bomb alerts, and it was followed by a series of bomb hoaxes that disrupted traffic in the provincial capital.

Politicians from the main pro-British Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) demanded an urgent meeting with police chiefs on Wednesday while a member of the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) said Britain must take on the guerrillas.
"The IRA are making it absolutely clear, for their part, that as far as they are concerned the war has started again," said DUP spokesman Gregory Campbell.

Urging Britain to stiffen resolve and not to give the IRA a voice in peace talks while its units wage war, Campbell said: "I think that the government should make it absolutely clear that they are now prepared to confront the IRA."

Campbell, speaking on BBC radio, suggested that Britain should reinstate checkpoints and high-level security at the border with the Irish Republic where control on crossing points was eased during a 17 month IRA truce that ended in February 1996.
In Belfast and Londonderry measures must be taken "to demonstrate to the people that the government are prepared to batten down the hatches and face the IRA," he said.

Five UUP members of the Northern Ireland Forum, an elected body boycotted by minority Irish Catholic nationalists, said they want to meet senior police to press for more patrols and other city-centre precautions to combat an IRA bombing threat.
"We don't want to see this city or Northern Ireland brought to a standstill. Nevertheless we need positive steps," UUP Forum member Jim Rodgers told Reuters.
Rodgers made a strong plea to pro-British Loyalist foes of the IRA not to end their 26-month ceasefire, a prospect that has sent shudders through leaders of the stalled peace process.

Pro-British militants are suspected of two revenge attacks on well-known Republicans, who oppose British rule and want an all-Ireland state ruled from Dublin. Parties linked to the banned Loyalists insist however that their truce is intact.
